head: 'Harringay' means the enclosure of a man called Hæring.
text: The same name gave Haringey and Hornsey, three spellings of one old word. Green Lanes was an old drovers' road for taking animals to London.

head: Named after Harrow and Wealdstone, the boundary stone of Harrow Weald.
text: 'Harrow' comes from Old English hearg, a heathen temple. 'Weald' means woodland, and the stone marked the edge of the woods north of Harrow. The station opened in 1837 on the London and Birmingham Railway.

head: 'Harrow' comes from Old English hearg, a heathen temple or shrine.
text: The shrine probably stood on top of the hill, where St Mary's Church stands today. The station opened in 1880 as Harrow and added 'on-the-Hill' in 1894.

head: 'Hatch End' means the district by the gate.
text: A hatch was a gate, probably into Pinner Park, a medieval deer park. Isabella Beeton, author of the famous Book of Household Management, lived here around 1860.

head: 'Hatton' means the farm on the heath.
text: The heath was Hounslow Heath, where Heathrow Airport now stands. 'Cross' probably refers to a crossroads.

head: 'Hayes' means land overgrown with brushwood; 'Harlington' the farm of Hygered's people.
text: Hayes comes from Old English hæs, brushwood. Harlington was recorded in 831 as Hygereding tun. Both villages are now next to Heathrow Airport.

head: Named after Headstone Manor, a moated manor house nearby.
text: Its oldest part dates from the 14th century, making it one of the oldest timber buildings in the area. It is now the museum of Harrow.

head: 'Heathrow' means the row of houses on the heath.
text: It was first recorded in 1410 as La Hetherewe, a hamlet on Hounslow Heath. Terminal 4 opened in 1986, with its own station on a loop of the Piccadilly line.

head: 'Heathrow' means the row of houses on the heath.
text: The hamlet, first recorded in 1410, disappeared when the airport was built in the 1940s. Terminal 5 and its station opened in 2008.

head: 'Heathrow' means the row of houses on the heath.
text: The station opened in 1977 as Heathrow Central. It became Heathrow Terminals 2 & 3 in 2016, after Terminal 1 closed.

head: 'Hendon' means at the high hill.
text: It was recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Hendun. The station opened in 1923.

head: Named after Heron Quays, a group of quays on the old West India Docks.
text: The quays were rebuilt in the 1980s as offices, beside Canary Wharf. The station opened with the first DLR line in 1987.

head: 'Barnet' means land cleared by burning.
text: It comes from Old English bærnet, burning. The town is also called Chipping Barnet, 'chipping' meaning a market. In 1471 the Battle of Barnet, part of the Wars of the Roses, was fought just north of the town.

head: 'Kensington' means the farm of a Saxon called Cynesige.
text: It is in the Domesday Book as Chenesitun. The station opened in 1868 on Kensington High Street, near Kensington Palace.

head: Named after the park of Highams, an 18th-century mansion.
text: 'Higham' means the high homestead. The grounds were landscaped by Humphry Repton in the 1790s.

head: 'Highbury' means the high manor; 'Islington' means the hill of a man called Gisla.
text: Islington was recorded around 1000 as Gislandune. Highbury was the higher of two manors in the parish. The Victoria line station opened in 1968.

head: Named after a high gate on the hill, a toll gate on the road north.
text: The gate led into the Bishop of London's hunting park, and travellers on the Great North Road paid a toll here. Highgate is one of the highest points in London.

head: 'Hillingdon' probably means the hill of a man called Hilla.
text: It is recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Hillendone, with -done meaning a hill. The station opened in 1923.

head: 'Holborn' probably means the stream in the hollow.
text: The stream was a tributary of the River Fleet, long since buried. Londoners traditionally say 'Hoe-bun'.

head: Named after Holland House, a 17th-century mansion whose grounds became the park.
text: The house took its name from Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, whose title came from Holland in Lincolnshire, not the Netherlands. Later the Fox family, Barons Holland, lived there.

head: 'Holloway' means the hollow way, a road worn deep into the ground.
text: Cattle and carts on their way to London's markets wore the road down over centuries. Another idea, a 'hallowed way' for pilgrims, is less likely.

head: 'Homerton' means the farm of a woman called Hūnburh.
text: It was recorded in 1343 as Hummerton. It is one of the few London names that recall a woman.

head: Named after the Oak of Honor on One Tree Hill.
text: Queen Elizabeth I is said to have rested under an oak on the hill on May Day 1602. An oak still stands there today.

head: 'Hornchurch' means the church with horns.
text: It was recorded in 1222. Nobody knows exactly why, but St Andrew's Church still has the head of a bull with real horns on its east end.

head: 'Hounslow' probably means the mound of the hound.
text: The 'hound' may be a dog or a man nicknamed Hund, and the mound probably a burial mound. The station opened in 1886 as Heston Hounslow and was renamed in 1925.

head: 'Hounslow' probably means the mound of the hound.
text: It ends in Old English hlāw, a mound or burial mound. The station was called Hounslow Town until 1925.

head: 'Hounslow' probably means the mound of the hound.
text: The station opened in 1884 as Hounslow Barracks, after the army barracks nearby, and was renamed Hounslow West in 1925.

head: 'Hoxton' means the farm of a man called Hōc.
text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Hochestone. In Shakespeare's time it was just outside the City, with fields and early theatres nearby.

head: Named after the corner of Hyde Park.
text: The park was once the manor of Hyde, owned by Westminster Abbey; 'hide' was an old measure of land. Henry VIII took it over in 1536 as a hunting ground.

head: 'Ickenham' means the homestead of a man called Ticca.
text: The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Ticheham; over time the T was lost. The village pump of 1866 still stands on the green.

head: 'Ilford' means the ford over the Hyle.
text: The Hyle, meaning 'the trickling stream', was the old name of the lower River Roding. Drop the H, and you have Ilford.

head: Named after a wharf of the Imperial Gas Works at Sands End, Fulham.
text: The Imperial Gas Light and Coke Company built a large gasworks by the river. The station opened in 2009.

head: Named after a small riverside park at the southern tip of the Isle of Dogs.
text: The park opened in 1895 and has a famous view across the Thames to Wren's Old Royal Naval College in Greenwich. A foot tunnel under the river, opened in 1902, starts here.

head: 'Iver' means the brow of a hill.
text: It comes from Old English yfer, the edge or brow of a slope. With four letters, it is one of the shortest station names in the London area.

head: 'Kennington' means the farm of a man called Cena.
text: It is recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Chenintune. Kennington Park was once a common where large public meetings were held.

head: 'Kensal' means the king's wood.
text: It was first recorded in the 13th century as Kingisholte. Nobody knows which king. The green lay where Kensal Green Cemetery, opened in 1833, is now.

head: 'Kensal' means the king's wood; a 'rise' is a slope.
text: It was first recorded in the 13th century as Kingisholte; nobody knows which king. The American writer Mark Twain opened Kensal Rise Library in 1900.

head: Named after Olympia, an exhibition hall opened in 1886.
text: The hall was probably named after Olympia in ancient Greece, home of the Olympic Games. Kensington means the farm of a Saxon called Cynesige. The station was called Kensington (Addison Road) until 1946.

head: Despite the name, Kentish Town has nothing to do with Kent, as far as anyone knows.
text: The name was recorded in 1208 as Kentisston. It may come from a family called Kentish, or from words describing the bed of a stream, the now-hidden River Fleet.

head: Despite the name, Kentish Town has nothing to do with Kent, as far as anyone knows.
text: It was recorded in 1208 as Kentisston. It may come from a family called Kentish, or from words for the bed of a stream, the now-hidden River Fleet.

head: 'Kenton' probably means the farm of a man called Coena.
text: It ends in Old English tūn, a farm or settlement. Bakerloo trains have called here since 1917.

head: Named after the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew.
text: 'Kew' was first recorded in 1327 as Cayho and probably means the spur of land by a landing place on the Thames. The gardens are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

head: 'Kilburn' probably means the cows' stream, or the royal stream.
text: The stream is the River Westbourne, now underground. It was first recorded in 1134 as Cuneburna. A priory stood where the Roman road crossed the stream.

head: 'Kilburn' probably means the cows' stream, or the royal stream.
text: The stream is the River Westbourne, now underground. Kilburn High Road follows the old Roman road, Watling Street.

head: 'Kilburn' probably means the cows' stream, or the royal stream.
text: The stream is the River Westbourne, now underground. 'Park' was added for the new housing estate. The station opened in 1915.

head: Named after King George V Dock, the last of the three Royal Docks.
text: It opened in 1921 and was named after the king of the time. The great ocean liners of the day used it.

head: Named after a statue of King George IV, and the church of St Pancras.
text: The area was once called Battle Bridge, after a crossing of the River Fleet. A monument to George IV stood here from about 1830 to 1845; it was unpopular and soon removed. St Pancras was a boy martyred in Rome, by tradition in 304.

head: 'Kingsbury' means the king's manor.
text: Nobody knows which king: by the time of the Domesday Book in 1086, the land was already in private hands. The station opened in 1932.

head: 'Knightsbridge' means the bridge of the young men.
text: Old English cniht meant a young man or servant, not yet a knight in armour. The bridge crossed the River Westbourne. The name was first recorded in about 1050.

head: Named after James Weller Ladbroke, who developed the area in the mid-19th century.
text: His family had owned the land since at least the early 17th century, and he named the main road after himself. The station opened in 1864 as Notting Hill.

head: 'Lambeth' means the landing place for lambs.
text: It was recorded in 1062 as Lambehitha: hithe is an old word for a landing place on a river, as in Rotherhithe. The station opened in 1906 and was renamed Lambeth North in 1917.

head: Named after the Lancaster Gate entrance to Kensington Gardens.
text: It was named in honour of Queen Victoria, who was also Duke of Lancaster. The city of Lancaster itself takes its name from a Roman fort, a 'caster', on the River Lune.

head: Named after Langdon Park, the small park next to the station.
text: While it was being built, the station was going to be called Carmen Street, after a road nearby.
